title: How do you manage Terraform module versioning and backward compatibility for modules consumed by many teams (SemVer releases — major = breaking, pin versions so prod never auto-consumes `latest`, a controlled upgrade process), and what counts as a breaking change (input/output changes, deprecated variables, resource renames that force state moves, Terraform/provider version bumps)?
shortTitle: Managing Terraform module versioning and backward compatibility for many-team modules, and what counts as a breaking change

s1_definition.profdef: Managing shared Terraform module versioning means publishing modules as immutable, semantically versioned releases (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), where MAJOR means a breaking change, MINOR means backward-compatible new features, and PATCH means backward-compatible fixes. Consumers pin to an exact or bounded version so production never automatically consumes the newest tag, and upgrades happen through a reviewed, tested process. A breaking change is anything that forces a consumer to edit their configuration or move state: renamed or removed input variables, changed output names or types, resource address renames that require state moves, and Terraform or provider version floors.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a central team that builds a reusable "vault blueprint" (a module) that every branch uses to build its own vault. If the central team changes the blueprint carelessly, every branch's vault could suddenly need rebuilding while Rajesh and Priya are mid-transaction. So the central team stamps each blueprint with a version number. A small fix that changes nothing for the branches gets a tiny bump. A new optional feature gets a medium bump. But if the new blueprint renames the vault door or removes a required measurement, that is a major version — branches must consciously opt in and adjust their plans. Each branch pins to the exact blueprint version it trusts, so no branch is ever upgraded behind its back.
s1_definition.oneliner: Publish modules with SemVer, pin consumers so prod never auto-takes latest, and treat any input/output rename, required state move, or version floor as a MAJOR breaking change.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Managing shared Terraform module versioning means publishing modules as immutable, semantically versioned releases (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), where MAJOR means a breaking change, MINOR means backward-compatible new features, and PATCH means backward-compatible fixes. Consumers pin to an exact or bounded version so production never automatically consumes the newest tag, and upgrades happen through a reviewed, tested process. A breaking change is anything that forces a consumer to edit their configuration or move state: renamed or removed input variables, changed output names or types, resource address renames that require state moves, and Terraform or provider version floors.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a central team that builds a reusable "vault blueprint" (a module) that every branch uses to build its own vault. If the central team changes the blueprint carelessly, every branch's vault could suddenly need rebuilding while Rajesh and Priya are mid-transaction. So the central team stamps each blueprint with a version number. A small fix that changes nothing for the branches gets a tiny bump. A new optional feature gets a medium bump. But if the new blueprint renames the vault door or removes a required measurement, that is a major version — branches must consciously opt in and adjust their plans. Each branch pins to the exact blueprint version it trusts, so no branch is ever upgraded behind its back.

**One line to remember:** Publish modules with SemVer, pin consumers so prod never auto-takes latest, and treat any input/output rename, required state move, or version floor as a MAJOR breaking change.

sections.s2_technical:
Semantic Versioning gives three numbers. The PATCH number (the third) increases for backward-compatible bug fixes — a consumer can take it with zero changes. The MINOR number (the second) increases for backward-compatible new features, such as adding a new optional input variable with a default, or a new output; existing consumers are unaffected. The MAJOR number (the first) increases for breaking changes — anything that forces consumers to edit their HCL or their state. The whole point of SemVer is that a consumer reading "4.1.2 to 4.3.0" knows it is safe, while "4.3.0 to 5.0.0" means read the upgrade guide carefully.

Pinning is how consumers protect themselves. In a module call you write `version = "4.2.1"` for an exact pin, or `version = "~> 4.2"` to accept any 4.2.x patch, or `version = ">= 4.2, < 5.0"` to accept minors but never the next major. The critical rule for production is to never leave the version unpinned and never point at a mutable branch like `main`, because then a module author's push could silently change your infrastructure. Private registries and Git tags give you immutable, versioned sources; a Git tag `?ref=v4.2.1` is immutable in a way that `?ref=main` is not.

What counts as a breaking change deserves precision. Renaming or removing an input variable is breaking, because every consumer passing that variable now errors. Changing a variable's type, or making an optional variable required, is breaking. Renaming or removing an output is breaking, because downstream code reading that output breaks. A resource address rename inside the module (for example moving `aws_instance.web` to `aws_instance.app`) is breaking because, without a `moved {}` block, Terraform sees the old address as destroyed and the new one as created — a recreation — and consumers must run a state move. Raising the minimum Terraform core version or the minimum provider version is breaking because consumers on older versions can no longer use the module. Even changing a default value can be breaking if it alters real infrastructure on the next apply.

A senior nuance: modern Terraform gives you tools to AVOID breaking changes where possible. A `moved {}` block lets you rename a resource inside the module and have Terraform automatically migrate state, so a rename that used to be breaking becomes a non-breaking minor. Deprecation is the polite path: instead of removing a variable in one release, you keep it for a major cycle, mark it deprecated in the docs and with a `validation` warning, and remove it only in the next major. You also publish a CHANGELOG and an UPGRADING guide for every major so the many teams consuming your module have a clear migration path. And you test the module in isolation with `terraform test` and example configurations before tagging a release.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's platform team owns a shared `networking` module used by twelve application teams, including the payments team that handles transfers between Rajesh SAV2001 and Priya CUR3001. The platform team wants to release changes without breaking those twelve teams.

Problem 1 — They add a new optional variable `enable_flow_logs` with a default of false. No existing team passes it, and the default keeps current behaviour. This is a backward-compatible feature, so it is a MINOR bump, and teams can upgrade freely.

Problem 2 — They rename an output from `subnet_id` to `private_subnet_id`. The payments team reads `module.networking.subnet_id` in their code, which would now fail. This is a breaking change requiring a MAJOR bump and an upgrade note.

Problem 3 — They want to rename an internal resource. Using a `moved {}` block they migrate state automatically, converting what would be a breaking recreation into a safe MINOR change.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `ModuleRegistry` that classifies a proposed change into PATCH, MINOR, or MAJOR, enforces that production consumers are pinned, and refuses to let a consumer auto-consume a MAJOR. Classes: `SemVer`, `ModuleChange` with a `ChangeKind`, `CompatibilityChecker` with `classify()` and `canAutoUpgrade()`, and a `ModuleVersioningDemo` main.

##### 4c. Configuration File — the real module call and a moved block

```hcl
# Consumer (payments team) — PINNED so prod never auto-takes a new MAJOR
module "networking" {
  source  = "git::https://git.nbi.internal/modules/networking.git?ref=v4.2.1"
  version = ">= 4.2, < 5.0"        # accept minors/patches, NEVER auto 5.x

  vpc_cidr         = "10.20.0.0/16"
  enable_flow_logs = true          # new optional var added in v4.2 (MINOR, safe)
}
```

```hcl
# Inside modules/networking/main.tf — a non-breaking rename using moved{}
moved {
  from = aws_subnet.internal      # old address
  to   = aws_subnet.private       # new address — state migrates automatically
}
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the shared networking module is at version 4.1.0 and the platform team has three proposed changes to release.

Step 1: The checker classifies the first change, adding an optional variable enable_flow_logs with a default of false. Because existing consumers are unaffected, this is a MINOR bump, taking the version from 4.1.0 to 4.2.0. Pinned consumers using the less-than-5.0 constraint can take it automatically and safely.

Step 2: The checker classifies the second change, an internal resource rename that uses a moved block. Because the moved block migrates state automatically, no consumer has to run a manual state move, so this is also a MINOR bump, from 4.2.0 to 4.3.0, and consumers auto-upgrade safely.

Step 3: The checker classifies the third change, renaming the output subnet_id to private_subnet_id. The payments team reads the old output name, so this change breaks their code. It is a MAJOR bump, from 4.3.0 to 5.0.0, and the gate refuses auto-upgrade — the twelve teams must read the upgrade guide and opt in by changing their pinned version.

Step 4: After all three changes, the module would be published as 5.0.0, with the first two changes safe and the last requiring a controlled opt-in migration.

  1. checker.classify(add optional input)        → MINOR
  2. checker.nextVersion(4.1.0, MINOR)            → 4.2.0; canAutoUpgrade → true
  3. checker.classify(rename WITH moved{})        → MINOR
  4. checker.nextVersion(4.2.0, MINOR)            → 4.3.0; canAutoUpgrade → true

sections.s6_takeaway:
Managing versioning for a Terraform module that many teams depend on comes down to Semantic Versioning plus disciplined pinning plus a controlled upgrade process. I publish every module as an immutable, versioned release in the form major-dot-minor-dot-patch. A patch is a backward-compatible bug fix, a minor is a backward-compatible new feature like adding an optional variable with a default, and a major is any breaking change. The value of this scheme is that a consumer reading the version jump knows instantly whether an upgrade is safe or needs care.

Pinning is how consumers stay safe. Every consumer pins to an exact tag or a bounded range such as greater-than-or-equal four-point-two and less-than five, and crucially never points at a mutable branch like main. That guarantees production never automatically consumes the latest tag, so a module author's push cannot silently change live infrastructure. Upgrades are always deliberate — a team edits its pinned version in a pull request, reviews the plan, and tests before applying.

What counts as a breaking change is the part interviewers probe. Removing or renaming an input variable is breaking because every consumer passing it now errors. Changing a variable's type or making an optional variable required is breaking. Renaming or removing an output is breaking because downstream code reading it fails. Renaming a resource inside the module is breaking because, without a moved block, Terraform treats it as a destroy and a create and consumers must run a state move. Raising the minimum Terraform or provider version is breaking too. In my project at the National Bank of India, our platform team owned a networking module used by twelve teams, including the payments team that handles transfers between Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001. Adding an optional flow-logs variable was a safe minor, and renaming an internal subnet resource was also kept non-breaking by using a moved block so state migrated automatically. But renaming the subnet_id output to private_subnet_id broke the payments team's code, so that went out as a major with a changelog and an upgrade guide, and the pinned consumers did not auto-upgrade — they opted in on their own schedule. The principle I always state is that backward compatibility is a contract, SemVer communicates it, and pinning enforces it.
